claim: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from 'emitting' plants inform the 'receiving' (listening) plants of impending stresses or simply of their presence.
source: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from 'emitting' plants inform the 'receiving' (listening) plants of impending stresses or simply of their presence.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant communication through VOCs, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The receptors that allow receiver plants to detect volatile cues are elusive.
source: However, the receptors that allow receivers to detect the volatile cue are elusive.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: Plants most likely have odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), similar to animals.
source: Most likely, plants (as animals) have odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), and in fact, a few OBPs are known to bind 'stress-induced' plant VOCs.
evidence: This is based on inference from animal biology and some existing evidence of plant OBPs.

claim: A few OBPs are known to bind 'stress-induced' plant VOCs.
source: Most likely, plants (as animals) have odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), and in fact, a few OBPs are known to bind 'stress-induced' plant VOCs.
evidence: This refers to existing knowledge in the literature about plant OBPs.

claim: Molecular docking simulation experiments suggest that structural features of a few plant proteins could allow VOC binding.
source: Molecular docking simulation experiments suggest that structural features of a few plant proteins screened in databases could allow VOC binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational docking experiments performed in the study.

claim: Monoterpenes may bind the same plant proteins that were described to bind other stress-induced VOCs.
source: In particular, our results show that monoterpenes may bind the same plant proteins that were described to bind other stress-induced VOCs, while the constitutive hemiterpene isoprene is unlikely to bind any investigated putative OBP and may not have an info-chemical role.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results presented in the study.

claim: The constitutive hemiterpene isoprene is unlikely to bind any investigated putative OBP.
source: In particular, our results show that monoterpenes may bind the same plant proteins that were described to bind other stress-induced VOCs, while the constitutive hemiterpene isoprene is unlikely to bind any investigated putative OBP and may not have an info-chemical role.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results showing high binding energy values for isoprene.

claim: Isoprene may not have an info-chemical role.
source: In particular, our results show that monoterpenes may bind the same plant proteins that were described to bind other stress-induced VOCs, while the constitutive hemiterpene isoprene is unlikely to bind any investigated putative OBP and may not have an info-chemical role.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the docking results and ecological observations.

claim: There may be plant OBPs that bind multiple VOCs, as for animals.
source: We conclude that, as for animal, there may be plant OBPs that bind multiple VOCs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the docking results and comparison with animal OBPs.

claim: Plant OBPs may play an important role in allowing plants to eavesdrop messages by neighboring plants, triggering defensive responses and communication with other organisms.
source: Plant OBPs may play an important role in allowing plants to eavesdrop messages by neighboring plants, triggering defensive responses and communication with other organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings and known plant communication mechanisms.

claim: Plants synthesize a variety of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are important for reproduction and defense and in general to communicate with other organisms.
source: Plants synthesize a variety of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are important for reproduction and defense and in general to communicate with other organisms (Ninkovic et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Insects and generalist herbivores, or carnivore insects that are also attracted by the volatile 'cry for help' released by plants upon herbivore attacks, are all able to sense plant volatiles.
source: Insects and generalist herbivores, or carnivore insects that are also attracted by the volatile 'cry for help' released by plants upon herbivore attacks, are all able to sense plant volatiles (Dicke and Loreto, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Whether volatiles are important in plant–plant communication is a fascinating, yet controversial, issue.
source: Whether volatiles are also important in plant–plant communication is a more fascinating, yet controversial, issue (Vickers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation indicating ongoing debate in the field.

claim: Growing reports show that VOCs influence plant–plant relationships.
source: Growing reports show that VOCs influence plant–plant relationships (Baldwin et al., 2002; Erb, 2019; Ninkovic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to existing literature.

claim: VOCs elicited in 'emitting' plants by abiotic or biotic stresses prime defensive responses in non-elicited 'receiving' plants.
source: VOCs elicited in 'emitting' plants by abiotic or biotic stresses prime defensive responses in non-elicited 'receiving' plants (Zuo et al., 2019; Frank et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: No study has so far looked for the primary events in plant–plant interaction, i.e., the receptors by which plants may sense VOCs emitted from neighboring plants are largely unknown.
source: However, no study has so far looked for the primary events in such elusive plant–plant interaction, i.e., the receptors by which plants may sense VOCs emitted from neighboring plants are largely unknown.
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It has been proposed that the passage of VOCs across the plasma membrane relies on their active transport.
source: Recently, it has been proposed that the passage of VOCs across the plasma membrane relies on their active transport.
evidence: This is based on existing proposals in the literature.

claim: The presence of an ABC carrier protein involved in active transport into plant cells has been hypothesized.
source: In particular, the presence of an ABC carrier protein involved in active transport into plant cells has been hypothesized (Adebesin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Plant VOC receptors may belong to a similar category of transporters.
source: Plant VOC receptors may belong to a similar category of transporters.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the ABC carrier hypothesis.

claim: An alternative explanation is that plants use odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) as protein carriers, alike animals.
source: An alternative explanation is that plants use odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) as protein carriers, alike animals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison with animal systems.

claim: There have been at least three cases in which the presence of OBPs was postulated in plants.
source: Indeed, there have been at least three cases in which the presence of OBPs was postulated in plants.
evidence: This is based on existing literature describing three plant proteins with OBP-like functions.

claim: COI1–JAZ is a high-affinity receptor protein for methyl-jasmonate (MeJa), the volatile moiety of jasmonic acid (JA).
source: (1) the COI1 assembly with a jasmonate zinc finger inflorescence meristem (ZIM)-domain (JAZ) protein family (COI1–JAZ), a high-affinity receptor protein for methyl-jasmonate (MeJa), and the volatile moiety of jasmonic acid (JA) (Sheard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: After JAZ degradation, transcription factors are released, which activate downstream genes and the defensive metabolites in plants challenged by abiotic and biotic stresses.
source: After JAZ degradation, transcription factors are released, which activate downstream genes and the defensive metabolites in plants challenged by abiotic and biotic stresses (Cheong and Choi, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: SABP2 is an esterase of the a/b-fold hydrolase superfamily that binds SA with high affinity.
source: (2) The salicylic acid (SA)-binding protein 2 (SABP2), an esterase of the a/b-fold hydrolase superfamily, that binds SA with high affinity and then converts the biologically inactive methyl ester of SA (MeSA) to active SA-inducing systemic acquired resistance in plants challenged by stresses (Park et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: SABP2 converts the biologically inactive methyl ester of SA (MeSA) to active SA-inducing systemic acquired resistance in plants challenged by stresses.
source: (2) The salicylic acid (SA)-binding protein 2 (SABP2), an esterase of the a/b-fold hydrolase superfamily, that binds SA with high affinity and then converts the biologically inactive methyl ester of SA (MeSA) to active SA-inducing systemic acquired resistance in plants challenged by stresses (Park et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: TPL specifically binds β-caryophyllene, a stress-induced sesquiterpene and a volatile signal for herbivores and carnivores in multitrophic interactions.
source: (3) The TOPLESS-like protein (TPL) that specifically binds β-caryophyllene, a stress-induced sesquiterpene and a volatile signal for herbivores and carnivores in multitrophic interactions.
evidence: This is based on existing literature about TPL function.

claim: TPL and TPL-related proteins are transcriptional co-repressors (also toward JA-mediated signaling).
source: TPL and TPL-related proteins are transcriptional co-repressors (also toward JA-mediated signaling).
evidence: This is based on existing knowledge about TPL function.

claim: Only the capacity to bind β-caryophyllene was tested with emitting and receiving (eavesdropping) plants for TPL.
source: Interestingly, only the capacity to bind β-caryophyllene was tested with emitting and receiving (eavesdropping) plants (Nagashima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: These three cases of plant OBPs need confirmation.
source: These three cases need confirmation, and all other plant VOCs (at least 1700 known so far; Dicke and Loreto, 2010) wait for identification of receptors (if present).
evidence: This reflects the authors' assessment of the current state of evidence.

claim: At least 1700 plant VOCs are known so far.
source: These three cases need confirmation, and all other plant VOCs (at least 1700 known so far; Dicke and Loreto, 2010) wait for identification of receptors (if present).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: The study focused on volatile isoprenoids (isoprene and monoterpenes) produced by the methyl erythritol phosphate (MEP) chloroplast pathway.
source: We focused on the volatile isoprenoids (isoprene and monoterpenes) produced by the methyl erythritol phosphate (MEP) chloroplast pathway and representing the largest component of plant VOC emissions in the atmosphere (Loreto and Schnitzler, 2010).
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: Volatile isoprenoids represent the largest component of plant VOC emissions in the atmosphere.
source: We focused on the volatile isoprenoids (isoprene and monoterpenes) produced by the methyl erythritol phosphate (MEP) chloroplast pathway and representing the largest component of plant VOC emissions in the atmosphere (Loreto and Schnitzler, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Approach (a) yielded five complete or partial protein sequences from plant databases.
source: Approach (a) yielded five complete or partial protein sequences, three from Anthurium amnicola (named OBP56d, OBP A10_1, and OBP A10_2), one from Nymphaea thermarum (named putative OBP), and one from Pyrus x bretschneideri (named OBP-70 like) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the results of the database search performed in the study.

claim: Statistically relevant similarity and coverage was only found between the putative OBP from N. thermarum and the Flowering locus T (FT) and T1 proteins, and the heading date 3A and 3B.
source: However, when these sequences were further screened for similarities with annotated plant proteins in the sequence databases, statistically relevant similarity and coverage was only found between the putative OBP from N. thermarum and the Flowering locus T (FT) and T1 proteins, and the heading date 3A and 3B.
evidence: This describes the results of sequence similarity analysis performed in the study.

claim: Comparison with animal OBPs yielded similarities between insect OBPs and plant OBP56d and OBP-70 like.
source: Comparison with animal OBPs, yielded similarities between (1) OBPs from insects and plant OBP56d and OBP-70 like, (2) chemosensor proteins and plant OBP A10_1, and (3) phosphatidylethanolamine-binding proteins and the putative OBP from N. thermarum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the results of comparative analysis performed in the study.

claim: Comparison with animal OBPs yielded similarities between chemosensor proteins and plant OBP A10_1.
source: Comparison with animal OBPs, yielded similarities between (1) OBPs from insects and plant OBP56d and OBP-70 like, (2) chemosensor proteins and plant OBP A10_1, and (3) phosphatidylethanolamine-binding proteins and the putative OBP from N. thermarum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the results of comparative analysis performed in the study.

claim: Comparison with animal OBPs yielded similarities between phosphatidylethanolamine-binding proteins and the putative OBP from N. thermarum.
source: Comparison with animal OBPs, yielded similarities between (1) OBPs from insects and plant OBP56d and OBP-70 like, (2) chemosensor proteins and plant OBP A10_1, and (3) phosphatidylethanolamine-binding proteins and the putative OBP from N. thermarum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the results of comparative analysis performed in the study.

claim: Only five animal protein families share sequence similarity with plant proteins.
source: Only five animal protein families share sequence similarity with plant proteins, as summarized in Table 1.
evidence: This is based on the BLAST comparison results presented in Table 1.

claim: Sequences were considered similar when showing BLAST E-values close to 0, and sequence identity ranges (20–45%) with a confident query coverage (highest values varying from 60% to 96%).
source: Sequences were considered similar when showing BLAST E-values close to 0, and sequence identity ranges (20–45%) with a confident query coverage (highest values varying from 60% to 96%).
evidence: This describes the criteria used in the study for determining sequence similarity.

claim: All plant protein sequences reported in Table 1 are related to inflorescence signaling.
source: Interestingly, all plant protein sequences reported in Table 1 are related to inflorescence signaling.
evidence: This is an observation based on the functional annotations of the proteins identified.

claim: HVA22 is induced by abscisic acid (ABA)/stress and has a role in the gibberellic acid (GA)-induced cellular death and in the regulation of seed germination.
source: HVA22 is induced by abscisic acid (ABA)/stress and has a role in the gibberellic acid (GA)-induced cellular death and in the regulation of seed germination (Shen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: FT is a florigen that induces and promotes the transition from vegetative growth to flowering.
source: FT is a florigen that induces and promotes the transition from vegetative growth to flowering (Koornneef et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: The protein MFT is involved in regulation of seeds germination by ABA/GA signaling.
source: The protein MFT is involved in regulation of seeds germination by ABA/GA signaling (Vaistij et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Heading date 3A-like is a probable florigen, which promotes the transition from vegetative growth to flowering downstream of HD1 and EHD1 under short day conditions.
source: Heading date 3A-like, as FT, is a probable florigen, which promotes the transition from vegetative growth to flowering downstream of HD1 and EHD1 under short day conditions (Taoka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Plant proteins previously reported in the literature (COI1–JAZ, SABP2, and TPL) were not retrieved by the search based on plant–animal protein similarities.
source: It is also remarkable that plant proteins previously reported in the literature (COI1–JAZ, SABP2, and TPL, see Introduction) were not retrieved by our search based on plant–animal protein similarities.
evidence: This describes a negative result from the database search performed in the study.

claim: Plant proteins may be able to work as OBPs even if different from animal OBPs, both at primary and tertiary structure levels.
source: This suggests that plant proteins may be able to work as OBPs even if different from animal OBPs, both at primary and tertiary structure levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that known plant OBPs were not retrieved by similarity searches.

claim: Nine putative plant OBPs were selected for molecular docking simulations.
source: This search was successful for nine putative plant OBPs that were then selected for molecular docking simulations of the interactions between potential plant OBPs and selected VOCs, to finally identify candidate plant OBPs.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study.

claim: α-pinene binds SABP2 with a binding energy value of −6.03 kcal/mol and a predicted Ki of 37 μM.
source: In our docking simulations, α-pinene seems to dock better on SABP2 and on the complete JA receptor, with binding energy value of −6.03 kcal/mol and −5.92 kcal/mol, and predicted Ki of 37 μM and 38.55 μM, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results presented in Table 2.

claim: α-pinene binds the complete JA receptor with a binding energy value of −5.92 kcal/mol and a predicted Ki of 38.55 μM.
source: In our docking simulations, α-pinene seems to dock better on SABP2 and on the complete JA receptor, with binding energy value of −6.03 kcal/mol and −5.92 kcal/mol, and predicted Ki of 37 μM and 38.55 μM, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results presented in Table 2.

claim: α-pinene binds the reference protein cytochrome P450 2B6 with an energy value of −5.42 kcal/mol and a predicted Ki of 103 μM.
source: For example, α-pinene binds the reference protein cytochrome P450 2B6 with an energy value of −5.42 kcal/mol and a predicted Ki of 103 μM.
evidence: This is based on the redocking simulation results for the reference complex.

claim: α-pinene binding to SABP2 and the complete JA receptor is better than the interaction with the reference complex.
source: In both cases, this is a better interaction than with the reference complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of binding energy values.

claim: β-myrcene binds SABP2, GA receptor, and the JA receptor better than the reference complex.
source: Similar to α-pinene, β-myrcene binds SABP2, GA receptor, and the JA receptor better than the reference complex.
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding energy values from the docking simulations.

claim: Protein heading date 3A, FT, and tfl1 showed binding energy values similar to the reference complex for β-myrcene.
source: Among the other candidate OBPs, protein heading date 3A, FT, and tfl1 showed binding energy values similar to the reference complex for β-myrcene.
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding energy values from the docking simulations.

claim: SABP2 showed energy values lower than the other candidate OBPs for limonene, and similar to the reference complex.
source: However, as in the previous cases, SABP2 showed energy values lower than the other candidate OBPs, and similar to the reference complex.
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding energy values from the docking simulations.

claim: β-caryophyllene showed the lowest binding energy values among the tested VOCs.
source: Remarkably, β-caryophyllene showed the lowest, and isoprene the highest, energy binding values.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results presented in Table 2.

claim: Isoprene showed the highest binding energy values among the tested VOCs.
source: Remarkably, β-caryophyllene showed the lowest, and isoprene the highest, energy binding values.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results presented in Table 2.

claim: The analysis confirms that OBPs might be present in plants.
source: Our analysis overall confirms that OBPs might be present in plants, and also bind VOCs produced by plants through the MEP pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the docking simulation results.

claim: Plant OBPs might bind VOCs produced by plants through the MEP pathway.
source: Our analysis overall confirms that OBPs might be present in plants, and also bind VOCs produced by plants through the MEP pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the docking simulation results.

claim: MEP synthesizes isoprenoids that are emitted constitutively (e.g. isoprene) or that are both constitutive and stress induced (e.g. monoterpenes).
source: MEP synthesizes isoprenoids that are emitted constitutively (e.g. isoprene) or that are both constitutive and stress induced (e.g. monoterpenes) (Dicke and Loreto, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Monoterpenes are efficiently bound by OBPs.
source: While monoterpenes are efficiently bound by OBPs, isoprene, the simplest and most abundantly emitted volatile isoprenoid, does not seem to bind strongly enough any OBP.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results showing low binding energy values for monoterpenes.

claim: Isoprene does not seem to bind strongly enough any OBP.
source: While monoterpenes are efficiently bound by OBPs, isoprene, the simplest and most abundantly emitted volatile isoprenoid, does not seem to bind strongly enough any OBP.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results showing high binding energy values for isoprene.

claim: Ecological observations report a role for monoterpenes in plant communication with other organisms.
source: Ecological observations report a role for monoterpenes in plant communication with other organisms (Bouwmeester et al., 2019), which is arguably not observed for isoprene (e.g. Brilli et al., 2009),
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: A role in plant communication with other organisms is arguably not observed for isoprene.
source: Ecological observations report a role for monoterpenes in plant communication with other organisms (Bouwmeester et al., 2019), which is arguably not observed for isoprene (e.g. Brilli et al., 2009),
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Isoprene influences many plant traits.
source: However, isoprene influences many plant traits (Monson et al., 2021) and profoundly modifies properties of cellular and sub-cellular membranes (Velikova et al., 2015; Pollastri et al., 2019), which may in turn activate signals reshaping plant genomes and phenomes (Harvey and Sharkey, 2016; Miloradovic van Doorn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Isoprene profoundly modifies properties of cellular and sub-cellular membranes.
source: However, isoprene influences many plant traits (Monson et al., 2021) and profoundly modifies properties of cellular and sub-cellular membranes (Velikova et al., 2015; Pollastri et al., 2019), which may in turn activate signals reshaping plant genomes and phenomes (Harvey and Sharkey, 2016; Miloradovic van Doorn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Isoprene modifications of membranes may activate signals reshaping plant genomes and phenomes.
source: However, isoprene influences many plant traits (Monson et al., 2021) and profoundly modifies properties of cellular and sub-cellular membranes (Velikova et al., 2015; Pollastri et al., 2019), which may in turn activate signals reshaping plant genomes and phenomes (Harvey and Sharkey, 2016; Miloradovic van Doorn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature and involves speculative reasoning.

claim: Isoprene is the main VOC emitted constitutively and not induced by stresses.
source: As isoprene is the main VOC emitted constitutively and not induced by stresses, it may be tempting to generalize from our observations that, unlike induced VOCs, constitutive VOCs are not bound by OBPs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about isoprene emission patterns.

claim: Unlike induced VOCs, constitutive VOCs may not be bound by OBPs.
source: As isoprene is the main VOC emitted constitutively and not induced by stresses, it may be tempting to generalize from our observations that, unlike induced VOCs, constitutive VOCs are not bound by OBPs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the docking results for isoprene.

claim: Monoterpenes seem to bind more efficiently with OBPs that are also reported to bind other plant volatiles.
source: Interestingly, monoterpenes seem to bind more efficiently with OBPs that are also reported to bind other plant volatiles.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results and comparison with known OBP functions.

claim: SABP2, the protein that strongly binds the stress-induced volatile MeSA, also seems to be a candidate for three tested monoterpenes.
source: In particular, SABP2, the protein that strongly binds the stress-induced volatile MeSA, also seems to be a candidate for three tested monoterpenes.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results showing low binding energy values for monoterpenes with SABP2.

claim: Protein heading date 3A and tfl1, GA receptor, and FT may bind, perhaps more specifically, the three monoterpenes.
source: Protein heading date 3A and tfl1, GA receptor, and FT may also bind, perhaps more specifically, the three monoterpenes.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results.

claim: The candidate plant OBPs have a broad ligand binding specificity and are likely to bind several different VOCs, as reported for OBPs from animals and insects.
source: Our results suggest that, as reported for the OBPs from animals and insects (Ramoni et al., 2007), the candidate plant OBPs have a broad ligand binding specificity and, consequently, they are likely to bind several different VOCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the docking results and comparison with animal OBPs.

claim: In many cases binding of the ligands occurs at the same protein structure site.
source: We noticed that in many cases binding of the ligands occurs at the same protein structure site, as shown for SABP2 in the experimentally reported complex with SA (Figure 1A), and in the simulated complexes with α-pinene, limonene, and β-myrcene (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on visual analysis of the docking simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The SABP2 binding site is characterized by the presence of aromatic side chains (two phenylalanines, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan).
source: The SABP2 binding site (represented in the right panels of Figure 1B–D) is characterized by the presence of aromatic side chains (two phenylalanines, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan), also observed in other candidate plant OBPs (GA receptor: two phenylalanines and four tyrosines; JA receptor: one phenylalanine, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan residue; FT receptor: two phenylalanines and one tryptophan).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites shown in Figure 1.

claim: The GA receptor binding site contains two phenylalanines and four tyrosines.
source: The SABP2 binding site (represented in the right panels of Figure 1B–D) is characterized by the presence of aromatic side chains (two phenylalanines, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan), also observed in other candidate plant OBPs (GA receptor: two phenylalanines and four tyrosines; JA receptor: one phenylalanine, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan residue; FT receptor: two phenylalanines and one tryptophan).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites.

claim: The JA receptor binding site contains one phenylalanine, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan residue.
source: The SABP2 binding site (represented in the right panels of Figure 1B–D) is characterized by the presence of aromatic side chains (two phenylalanines, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan), also observed in other candidate plant OBPs (GA receptor: two phenylalanines and four tyrosines; JA receptor: one phenylalanine, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan residue; FT receptor: two phenylalanines and one tryptophan).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites.

claim: The FT receptor binding site contains two phenylalanines and one tryptophan.
source: The SABP2 binding site (represented in the right panels of Figure 1B–D) is characterized by the presence of aromatic side chains (two phenylalanines, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan), also observed in other candidate plant OBPs (GA receptor: two phenylalanines and four tyrosines; JA receptor: one phenylalanine, one tyrosine, and one tryptophan residue; FT receptor: two phenylalanines and one tryptophan).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites.

claim: The ABA receptor has one phenylalanine and one tyrosine in the binding site.
source: Other candidate plant OBPs have some aromatic side chains in the binding site, although in lower number (e.g., the ABA receptor has one phenylalanine and one tyrosine, while TLF1 has two phenylalanines).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites.

claim: TLF1 has two phenylalanines in the binding site.
source: Other candidate plant OBPs have some aromatic side chains in the binding site, although in lower number (e.g., the ABA receptor has one phenylalanine and one tyrosine, while TLF1 has two phenylalanines).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding sites.

claim: The presence of aromatic side chains in binding sites is reminiscent of the binding site of OBPs from animal organisms.
source: This is also reminiscent of the binding site of OBPs from animal organisms (Bianchet et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on comparison with animal OBPs and supported by a citation.

claim: Bovine OBPs include five phenylalanines and one tyrosine.
source: Bovine OBPs include five phenylalanines and one tyrosine; Drosophila OBPs have four phenylalanines and one tryptophan; and porcine OBPs have two phenylalanines.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about animal OBPs.

claim: Drosophila OBPs have four phenylalanines and one tryptophan.
source: Bovine OBPs include five phenylalanines and one tyrosine; Drosophila OBPs have four phenylalanines and one tryptophan; and porcine OBPs have two phenylalanines.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about animal OBPs.

claim: Porcine OBPs have two phenylalanines.
source: Bovine OBPs include five phenylalanines and one tyrosine; Drosophila OBPs have four phenylalanines and one tryptophan; and porcine OBPs have two phenylalanines.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about animal OBPs.

claim: A hydrophobic environment where odorant molecules can be accommodated is needed for OBP function.
source: This conserved feature across biomes may reveal that a hydrophobic environment where odorant molecules can be accommodated is needed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conserved presence of aromatic residues in OBP binding sites.

claim: Larger ligands may interact with additional aromatic or hydrophobic side chains in the binding pockets.
source: Analysis of the β-caryophyllene complexes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) also suggests that larger ligands may interact with additional aromatic or hydrophobic side chains in the binding pockets.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the docking results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plant OBPs may be structurally and functionally similar to OBPs described in animals.
source: Overall, our study confirms that plant OBPs may exist and that they may be structurally and functionally similar to OBPs described in animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Plant OBPs seem to be able to bind different VOCs in the same binding site, using the same amino acid sequences, as in the case of animal OBPs.
source: As in the case of animal OBPs, also plant OBPs seem to be able to bind different VOCs in the same binding site, using the same amino acid sequences.
evidence: This is based on the docking simulation results and comparison with animal OBPs.

claim: Plant OBPs have both common and different features compared to animal OBPs.
source: While our in silico results make the case that plants also have OBPs, with both common and different features compared to animal OBPs, functional validation should follow.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative analysis performed in the study.

claim: Chemical synthesis of fluorescent VOCs could be used to confirm VOC binding by putative OBPs and to characterize protein–ligand binding mechanisms and sites.
source: For example, chemical synthesis of fluorescent VOCs could be used to confirm VOC binding by putative OBPs and to characterize protein–ligand binding mechanisms and sites.
